¶
{{smaller block|'''Avast heaving''' (''naut.''), the cry to arrest the capstan when nippers are jammed, or any other impediment occurs in heaving the cable.}}

'''avatar''' (av-ạ-tär′ or av′ạ-tär), ''n.'' [< Skt. ''avatāra'', descent, < ''ava'', down, + √ ''tar'', cross over, pass through.] '''1.''' In ''Hindu myth.'', the descent of a deity to the earth in an incarnate form or some manifest shape; the incarnation of a god.
{{smaller block|Three of the ''Avatāras'' or incarnations of Vishnu are connected with a deluge, . . . Vishnu in each case rescuing mankind from destruction by water.
{{right|''Max Müller'', India, p. 144.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' A remarkable appearance, manifestation, or embodiment of any kind; a descent into a lower sphere; an adorable or wonderful exhibition of an abstract idea, principle, etc., in concrete form: as, “The Irish ''Avatar''” (a poem by Byron on a visit of George IV. to Ireland); “the ''avatar'' of mathematics,” ''Masson'', Milton, I. 226.
{{smaller block|[Carlyle is] the most shining ''avatar'' of whim the world has ever seen.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 148.}}}}

'''avatara''' (av-ạ-tä′rä̤), ''n.'' Same as ''avatar''.

'''avaunce†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''advance''.

'''avaunt<sup>1</sup>''' (a-vänt′ or -vânt′), ''adv.'' and ''interj.'' [ME., < OF. ''avant'', forward, < LL. ''abante'', lit. from before: see ''avant-''.] '''I.†''' ''adv.'' Forward.
{{smaller block|And with that word came Drede ''avaunt''.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 3958.}}}}

'''II.''' ''interj.'' Away! begone! depart! an exclamation of contempt or abhorrence.
{{smaller block|''Avaunt'', thou hateful villain, get thee gone!
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 3.}}}}

'''avaunt<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [< ''avaunt''<sup>1</sup>, ''interj.''] Dismissal.

To give her the ''avaunt!'' It is a pity
Would move a monster.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 3.}}}}</poem>

'''avaunt<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. i.'' [A modification of ''avance''<sup>1</sup> = ''advance'', due to influence of ''avaunt''<sup>1</sup>, ''adv.''] To advance.
{{smaller block|''Avaunting'' in great bravery. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iii. 6.}}}}

'''avaunt<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v.'' [ME. ''avaunten'', ''avanten'', < OF. ''avanter'', ''avaunter'', < ''a-'' + ''vanter'', ''vaunter'', vaunt: see ''vaunt'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To praise highly; vaunt; make renowned.
{{smaller block|Do you favour you to ''avaunte.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1788.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' or ''reflexive.'' To boast; brag; speak or express vauntingly.
{{smaller block|<poem>“Thanne,” quod she, “I dar ''me'' wel ''avaunte'',
Thy lif is sauf.” ''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 158.</poem>
Let now the papists ''avaunt themselves!''
{{right|''Cranmer'', Ans. to Gardiner, p. 333.}}}}

'''avaunt<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''avaunt''; < ''avaunt''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] A boast; a vaunt.—'''To make avaunt''', {{smaller|to assert confidently; declare positively. ''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 289.}}

'''avauntance†''', ''n.'' [ME., < ''avaunten'': see ''avaunt''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.'', and ''-ance''. Cf. OF. ''vantance'', < ''vanter'', vaunt.] Boasting.

'''avaunter†''', '''avauntour†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''avauntour'', ''avaunter'', < OF. ''avantour'', ''-eor'', < ''avanter'': see ''avaunt''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] A boaster.
{{smaller block|<poem>He is not nyce
Ne ''avauntour.'' ''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 724.</poem>}}

¶
'''avauntry†''', ''n.'' [ME., also ''avauntarie'', < OF. *''avanterie'', found only as ''vanterie'': see ''avaunt''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] Same as ''avauntance''.

'''avdp.''' An abbreviation of ''avoirdupois''.

'''ave''' (ā′vē or ä′ve), ''interj.'' [L., hail! orig. impv. of ''avere'', be well, be of good cheer; esp. in LL. phrase ''Ave Maria'', hail Mary! in allusion to Luke i. 28: “''Ave'' [''Maria''], gratia plena.”] Hail! Also, farewell!
{{smaller block|<poem>And “''Ave, Ave, Ave''” said,
“Adieu, adieu” for evermore.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lvii.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Ave Maria,''' the Hail Mary, a devotion or prayer used in the Western Church. In the older form it consists of the salutation of the angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary when he announced to her the incarnation (Luke i. 28), together with the words of Elizabeth to Mary (Luke i. 42). This form of the Hail Mary was used as an anthem in both the Eastern and Western churches as early as the seventh century. It came into wide use as a devotion in the eleventh century. The concluding words, “Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us,” etc., were first introduced in the fifteenth century, and first authorized for daily use in the breviary in 1568. Also called the ''angelic salutation''. See ''angelus''.}}

'''ave''' (ā′vē or ä′ve), ''n.'' [< ''ave'', ''interj.''] '''1.''' An Ave Maria (which see, under ''ave'', ''interj.'').
{{smaller block|<poem>Nine hundred Pater nosters every day,
And thrise nine hundred ''Aves'' she was wont to say.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iii. 13.}}}}
'''2.''' A salutation.
{{smaller block|Their loud applause and ''aves'' vehement.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 1.}}}}

readings.c2s2:
''Maria'' (which see, under ''ave'', ''interj.'').
{{smaller block|<poem>He told of Saintes and Popes, and evermore
He strowd an ''Ave-Mary'' after and before.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. i. 35.}}
I could never hear the ''Ave-Mary'' bell without an elevation, or think it a sufficient warrant because they erred in one circumstance for me to err in all—that is, in silence and dumb contempt.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, i. § 3.}}}}

'''Avena''' (a̤-vē′nä̤), ''n.'' [L., oats.] A genus of plants, natural order ''Gramineæ'', characterized by having large membranous outer glumes, which inclose two or three perfect flowers, each with a long, bent, and twisted awn on the back of the lower palet. {{smaller|The species are natives of temperate and cold regions. Some are useful pasture-grasses, but by far the most important species is ''A. sativa'', the cultivated oat. See ''oat''.}}

'''avenaceous''' (av-ẹ̄-nā′shius), ''a.'' [< L. ''avenaceus'', < ''avena'', oats.] Belonging to or resembling oats.

'''avenage''' (av′ẹ̄-nạ̄j), ''n.'' [< OF. ''avenage'', < ''avene'', oats, < L. ''avena'', oats.] In ''old law'', a certain quantity of oats paid by a tenant to a landlord in lieu of rent or other duty.

'''avenary†''' (av′ẹ̄-nā-ri), ''n.'' [< L. ''avenarius'', < ''avena'', oats.] Same as ''avener''.

'''avenaunt†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''avenant'', ''avenand'', etc., < OF. (and mod. F.) ''avenant'', comely, convenient, ppr. of ''avenir'', come, suit, become, < L. ''advenire'', come: see ''advene'', and cf. ''convenient'', ''comely'', and ''becoming''.] '''1.''' Becoming; well-looking.
{{smaller block|<poem>Clere browne she was, and thereto bright
Of face, body ''avenaunt''. ''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 1263.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Convenient; suitable.
readings.c3s2:
after ''vengeance.''] The act of avenging; vengeance: as, “fear signal ''avengeance,''” ''J. Philips'', Cyder, ii. 49.

'''avengeful''' (a̤-venj′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''avenge'', ''n.'', + ''-ful'', after ''revengeful.''] Avenging; executing vengeance. [Rare.]

'''avengement''' (a̤-venj′mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''avenge'' + ''-ment.''] The act of avenging; vengeance; punishment; satisfaction taken. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Nought may thee save from heavens ''avengëment.''
{{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos.}}
God’s ''avengement'' of his repulse at Hull.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes.}}}}

'''avenger''' (a̤-ven′jėr), ''n.'' One who avenges or takes vengeance.
{{smaller block|The Lord is the ''avenger'' of all such. 1 Thes. iv. 6.
Brutus, thou saint of the ''avenger’s'' order.
{{right|''Beddoes'', Death’s Jest-Book, i. 1.}}}}

'''avengeress''' (a̤-ven′jėr-es), ''n.'' [< ''avenger'' + ''-ess.''] A female avenger. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|That cruell Queene ''avengeresse.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. viii. 20.}}}}

'''aveniform''' (a̤-vē′ni-fôrm), ''a.'' [< L. ''avena'', oats, + ''forma'', form.] Resembling a grain of oats. ''Thomas'', Med. Dict.

'''avenin''' (a̤-vē′nin), ''n.'' [< L. ''avena'', oats, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.] A nitrogenous proteid substance found in oats, similar to legumin, and probably a mixture of legumin and gluten.

'''avenious''' (a̤-vē′ni-us), ''a.'' Same as ''avenous.''

'''avenor†''', ''n.'' See ''avener.''

'''avenous''' (a̤-vē′nus), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἀ- priv. + L. ''vena'', vein.] In ''bot.'', wanting veins or nerves, as the leaves of certain plants. Also ''avenious.''
